name: Dyslexia
summary: Dyslexia is characterised primarily by persistent difficulties with word reading and/or spelling, with presentation and impact varying across people, writing systems, tasks and support contexts.

includes: Persistent difficulties with word reading and spelling, including accuracy, speed or both.
Variation across writing systems, age, task demands and support contexts.
Assessment boundaries, co-occurrence and practical access needs across childhood and adulthood.
excludes: Using low reading attainment alone as proof of dyslexia.
Using general intelligence or an IQ discrepancy as a simple eligibility test for dyslexia.
Treating every difficulty with memory, planning, attention, writing or mathematics as a core feature of dyslexia.
Individual diagnosis or universal intervention recommendations.

claims.text: Dyslexia is characterised primarily by persistent difficulty with word reading and/or spelling, involving accuracy, speed or both, and its presentation can vary with the writing system.
Dyslexic word-level literacy difficulties occur across a range of cognitive profiles, so general intelligence should not be used as a simple test of whether someone can be dyslexic.
Dyslexic difficulties can continue into adulthood, while their practical impact varies with the person, task, environment, expectations and available support.

sources.citation: International Dyslexia Association. 2025 Dyslexia Definition Project; definition adopted 22 October 2025.
Catts HW, Haynes CW, Joshi RM. Defining dyslexia: 2025 revision. Annals of Dyslexia. 2026.
British Dyslexia Association. My Dyslexia Story: Rebecca Harrison-Ruddock. 26 May 2026.

uncertainties.question: How should dyslexia be described and assessed across different languages and writing systems?
uncertainties.why_it_matters: The most visible English-language features are not equally prominent in every orthography, so an English-centred description can become falsely universal.
what_would_reduce_it: Cross-linguistic consensus reviews and assessment guidance covering multiple orthographies and multilingual learners.

uncertainties.question: Which assessment approaches most reliably distinguish dyslexia from other causes of reading difficulty without relying on unsupported IQ-discrepancy rules?
uncertainties.why_it_matters: Assessment practice remains diverse, and a public definition should not silently become a diagnostic algorithm.
what_would_reduce_it: Current multidisciplinary assessment consensus with evidence on diagnostic validity across ages and settings.

uncertainties.question: Which commonly reported non-reading difficulties should be treated as core dyslexia features rather than co-occurring or secondary experiences?
uncertainties.why_it_matters: Over-broad descriptions can make dyslexia an explanation for unrelated difficulties and erase useful distinctions between conditions.
what_would_reduce_it: High-quality factor, longitudinal and co-occurrence evidence separating core, associated and secondary features.

perspectives.held_by: Some dyslexic people and dyslexia advocates
perspectives.summary: Dyslexia may be experienced as both a source of real literacy barriers and part of a valued neurodivergent identity; individual strengths should not be universalised into a claim that every dyslexic person has the same compensating gifts.

relations.note: Current dyslexia definition work recognises ADHD as a distinct condition that can co-occur with dyslexia; this does not imply shared diagnosis or cause.
DLD and dyslexia can overlap in developmental language and literacy profiles, but they remain distinct candidate concepts.

questions: Which adjustments reduce avoidable reading and writing barriers at school, university and work?
When are assistive technologies useful, and what task are they solving?
Who performs a dyslexia assessment in the UK, and what can an assessment establish or not establish?
Which organisations provide evidence-based information, rights guidance and lived-experience support?

provenance.method: Candidate-only evidence synthesis from current NHS guidance, the 2025 IDA definition and 2026 peer-reviewed definition paper, plus bounded lived-experience material; not promoted to the authoritative corpus.
